strengths: Addresses an important problem—generalization in robotic grasping—with a cognitively inspired training paradigm using randomly composed primitive toys.
Extensive experimental evaluation across simulation, a real Franka robot, and a humanoid dexterous-hand platform, with comparisons to large vision-language-action baselines.
DetPool is a simple, lightweight mechanism that yields substantial improvements over standard pooling baselines in ablation studies.
Includes useful scaling studies, primitive/complexity ablations, and detailed reproducibility resources such as code, checkpoints, dataset, and hardware/printing specifications.
Reports a promising 67% zero-shot success rate on 64 real YCB objects, demonstrating data-efficient generalization from toy training.
weaknesses: The central claim of outperforming state-of-the-art methods is overstated: on the real Franka, finetuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56% versus LEGO's 66.67%, which the abstract does not mention. The abstract also claims 'outperforming state-of-the-art approaches that rely on substantially more in-domain data,' but this does not hold against the finetuned π0-FAST.

Table 2 marks LEGO as having no pretraining, but the method uses a pretrained MVP vision encoder, SAM 2 for segmentation, and a detector backbone. This is misleading and undermines claims about training from scratch.

The key mechanism of DetPool is not fully isolated: there is no ablation for object-token pooling without the attention mask, so it is unclear whether the attention masking or simply pooling object-masked tokens drives the gains. A comparison to cropping the object region is also missing.

DetPool depends critically on accurate object masks at test time. Simulation uses ground-truth masks (an oracle), while real experiments use a detector trained only on 200 toy images plus SAM 2. Detection/mask quality on YCB objects is never evaluated, making real-world results hard to interpret.

Baseline implementations appear suboptimal or unfair: π0-FAST and OpenVLA-OFT show extremely low and degrading performance in simulation, raising concerns that comparisons do not reflect their true capabilities. Comparisons to state-of-the-art grasping-specific methods (e.g., AnyGrasp, GraspNet) are absent.

The real Franka evaluation seems to use single-object placements rather than cluttered scenes, whereas the simulation uses a cluttered YCB setting. This reduces the difficulty of the real-world generalization claim and differs from the challenging setting emphasized in the abstract.

The scaling study confounds toy diversity with demonstrations per toy: varying the number of unique toys while keeping total demonstrations fixed changes the number of demonstrations per toy, so the claim that diversity and demonstration count both matter is not cleanly isolated.

No error bars or statistical significance tests are reported for success rates. This is especially problematic for the humanoid experiments with only 13 objects and 5 trials each, further weakened by reported hardware issues such as unresponsive thumb joints.

The title and abstract overclaim with 'Grasp Anything' and 'outperforming state-of-the-art,' while the evaluation is limited to YCB and 13 everyday objects and does not establish broad generalization to arbitrary objects.

strengths: Addresses an important and interesting question: whether a grasping policy trained only on simple, randomly composed primitive toys can zero-shot generalize to real-world objects.
Substantial real-robot effort, including evaluations on a Franka arm with a gripper and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands, which is more than many simulation-only papers.
Provides systematic ablations over the number of toys, number of demonstrations, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, and color, giving useful empirical insight into scaling behavior.
The proposed DetPool mechanism is simple and shows large gains over standard pooling baselines in simulation, suggesting that object-focused visual features matter for this setting.
Reproducibility details are extensive: 3D printing settings, hardware configurations, baseline implementation details, and a stated project page with code/checkpoints/dataset.
weaknesses: The central claim is substantially overstated. The abstract and conclusion imply that LEGO outperforms state-of-the-art approaches relying on more in-domain data, but in the real Franka experiment the finetuned π0-FAST baseline achieves 76.56% versus LEGO's 66.67%. LEGO only beats zero-shot π0-FAST and weaker baselines, so the headline claim is not supported by the main real-world result.

DetPool relies on external object segmentation/detection (SAM 2 plus a Faster R-CNN detector, and ground-truth masks in simulation) and essentially performs masked mean pooling over object patches. The pooling baselines do not receive object masks, so the comparison is not apples-to-apples; much of the gain may come from privileged object localization rather than from a novel object-centric learning mechanism.

The method is incremental: random primitive toys + segmentation-based masked attention/pooling + ViT encoder + transformer behavior cloning. The paper does not provide a deep analysis of why DetPool works, nor does it compare against other object-centric or data-efficient manipulation methods such as OTTER, ACT, Diffusion Policy, or other representation-learning baselines.

The VLA baselines are likely disadvantaged by being finetuned on very small datasets for which they were not designed; their poor simulation performance (e.g., π0-FAST at 4–8%) makes the comparison unconvincing as evidence of LEGO's superiority over specialized grasping methods.

Evaluation lacks statistical rigor: no confidence intervals or significance tests, no per-object breakdown for the YCB results, and no analysis of detector/segmentation accuracy or sensitivity to mask errors. The H1-2 humanoid result uses only 5 trials per object and was affected by hardware issues, so the reported 50.77% is noisy.

Experimental setups are inconsistent across methods. LEGO uses only two tabletop cameras in the real Franka setting, while baselines use wrist/head cameras and different action parameterizations (absolute vs delta joint control, language instructions). This confounds the comparison.

The title and framing ('Grasp Anything') are broader than the actual scope: the method is evaluated only on single-step grasping of rigid YCB-like objects, with limitations acknowledged but not reflected in the main claims.

There is no comparison to simpler alternatives such as cropping the input to the detected object or feeding object masks to baseline policies. Without such controls, it is unclear whether DetPool's benefit is due to the proposed mechanism or merely due to object isolation.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem: zero-shot generalization from randomly composed primitive toys to real-world YCB objects, inspired by cognitive science and Cézanne's primitive-shape idea.

Simple and effective object-centric representation via DetPool: using segmentation masks to restrict ViT attention to object patches and mean-pooling object tokens yields large gains over standard pooling baselines.
Comprehensive empirical study: scaling with toy diversity/demonstrations, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, and color, plus simulation and real-robot evaluations.

Strong data efficiency: an 86M model trained from scratch on 1,500 real demonstrations achieves 66.67% success on 64 YCB objects, outperforming much larger OpenVLA-OFT and zero-shot π0-FAST and ShapeGrasp baselines.
Reproducibility: project page with code, checkpoints, dataset, and detailed appendices covering hardware, toy manufacturing, baseline implementation, training, and evaluation protocols.
Cross-embodiment evidence: results on a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands demonstrate potential beyond a single robot setup.
weaknesses: Abstract/conclusion overclaim: the paper states it outperforms state-of-the-art approaches relying on more in-domain data, but finetuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56% versus LEGO's 66.67% on real Franka YCB; LEGO only outperforms zero-shot π0-FAST and OpenVLA-OFT.

Reliance on object segmentation masks at both training and test time: real-world masks are obtained via a Faster R-CNN trained on 200 toy images plus SAM 2, but it is unclear how well this detector generalizes to novel YCB objects, and sensitivity to mask errors is not studied.

Fairness of large VLA baselines is not fully established: finetuning 3B/7B pretrained models on a small toy dataset with potentially mismatched language instructions and action spaces may disadvantage them; OpenVLA-OFT's degradation with more data is suspicious.

Limited methodological novelty: DetPool is a straightforward combination of segmentation masks, attention masking, and mean pooling, conceptually related to prior object-centric and OTTER-style approaches; the main contribution is largely empirical.

Real-world evaluation is narrow: Franka tests place single objects on a predefined grid, and H1-2 tests only 13 objects with 5 trials each on the left hand, providing limited evidence for clutter, target selection, or dynamic scenes.

No evaluation of generalization to deformable, articulated, or physically diverse objects, and no analysis of how DetPool's benefit relates to privileged mask information versus the representation itself.

strengths: Interesting and well-motivated idea: training on random compositions of four shape primitives ('Cézanne toys') to induce zero-shot grasping generalization, inspired by cognitive science and Cézanne.

Simple and effective object-centric representation (DetPool) that restricts ViT attention to object patches via a segmentation mask and mean-pools object tokens; ablations show improvement over standard pooling baselines.

Extensive evaluation across simulation (ManiSkill/YCB), a real Franka arm with 64 YCB objects, and a Unitree H1-2 humanoid with dexterous hands, reporting strong zero-shot success rates in several settings.

Thorough empirical studies: scaling with toy diversity and demonstrations, model size, primitive types, toy complexity, geometric similarity, and robustness to lighting, clutter, distractors, and mask noise.
Good reproducibility effort: code, checkpoints, and dataset promised; hardware setup, 3D-printing parameters, baseline implementation details, and evaluation protocols are documented.
Demonstrates data efficiency and cross-embodiment generalization with an 86M-parameter policy, smaller than the VLA baselines considered.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: DetPool is essentially segmentation-guided masked attention plus mean pooling over object tokens, and object-centric representations / mask-based pooling are already known. The toy-training idea is conceptually interesting but not a fundamentally new algorithm.

Overclaimed state-of-the-art performance: on the real Franka benchmark, finetuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56% versus LEGO's 66.67%, yet the abstract and introduction emphasize outperforming SOTA without clearly qualifying that the finetuned π0-FAST is best. The claim of being 'trained from scratch' is also misleading because MVP ViT-L and SAM2 are pretrained.

Mask acquisition for real-world novel objects is under-specified and potentially not fully zero-shot: a Faster R-CNN detector is trained on 200 toy images and then used with SAM2 for YCB objects, with no detection/mask quality metrics or clear target-object selection in clutter. DetPool's generalization depends heavily on this pipeline.

Baseline comparisons may be unfair or inconsistent: OpenVLA-OFT uses delta control while LEGO uses absolute control (shown much better in Table 16), and the simulation success threshold is lowered for OpenVLA-OFT. OpenVLA-OFT's performance degrading with more data suggests training or action-space issues rather than a clean generalization comparison.

Some ablation interpretations are inconsistent or unsupported: primitive-removal results vary with demonstration count (cuboid removal hurts most at 100 demos, sphere later), the toy-complexity table shows five-primitive-only training performs poorly rather than clearly 'beneficial', and the geometric-similarity table reports slightly higher success for hard objects than easy objects.
The H1-2 humanoid evaluation is small (13 objects × 5 trials, left arm only, hardware issues) and lacks confidence intervals; real Franka results also lack variance estimates.

The DetPool ablation does not fully isolate the attention-mask component from object-token pooling, since the compared pooling baselines also change how tokens are attended and pooled, leaving the exact source of improvement somewhat entangled.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: zero-shot generalization for robotic grasping from limited, synthetic training objects.
Includes both simulation and real-world experiments on two robot embodiments (Franka gripper and Unitree H1-2 dexterous hands), which is a substantial experimental effort.
The proposed DetPool mechanism is simple and, within the reported experiments, yields strong improvements over several pooling baselines.
Provides extensive appendix material on toy generation, 3D printing, teleoperation, and training details, and promises code/checkpoints/dataset.
The Cézanne-toy idea is conceptually interesting and may inspire future work on compositional generalization in manipulation.
weaknesses: The central claim is overstated and inconsistent with the results: the abstract claims outperforming state-of-the-art approaches, but on the real Franka benchmark finetuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56% vs. LEGO's 66.67%. LEGO only outperforms zero-shot π0-FAST and poorly tuned OpenVLA-OFT/ShapeGrasp, so the headline claim is not supported.

The comparison is not controlled for input information: DetPool uses a target-object segmentation mask to restrict attention and pool object tokens, while baselines receive full images without equivalent object masks or crops. This gives LEGO a privileged object-centric input and confounds the attribution of gains to DetPool.

The real-world segmentation pipeline is under-specified and potentially invalid: the detector is trained on only 200 toy images, but evaluation is on YCB objects. There is no evaluation of mask quality or detector generalization to YCB, and target selection in clutter/multi-object scenes is not explained.

Baseline training appears unreliable: in simulation, OpenVLA-OFT performance degrades sharply as more demonstrations are added (36.35% at 500 demos to 12.79% at 2500 demos), suggesting under-tuning or overfitting rather than a fair comparison. For H1-2, π0-FAST uses delta control while LEGO uses absolute control, making the comparison less apples-to-apples.

The scaling study confounds object diversity with demonstrations per object. Fixing the total number of demonstrations while varying unique toys means that with 1000 toys each toy receives only 2.5 demonstrations, whereas with 15 toys each receives many more. The conclusion that demonstration count is more critical than diversity is therefore not well supported.

The novelty of DetPool is limited: using a segmentation mask to restrict ViT attention and mean-pool object tokens is a straightforward combination of existing object-centric attention and pooling ideas. The paper does not sufficiently position this against prior object-centric manipulation methods beyond a brief related-work discussion.

Evaluation is narrow and lacks statistical rigor. Only selected graspable YCB objects and 13 everyday objects are tested; H1-2 results use only 5 trials per object, and no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported, making the claimed superiority fragile.

The paper contains numerous presentation and reproducibility issues: malformed tables, citation errors (e.g., π0-FAST cited as Black et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2024), typos, and missing details about target mask acquisition and baseline tuning. These issues make the work harder to assess and reproduce.

strengths: The paper presents a novel and well-motivated paradigm: training grasping policies on randomly composed toys made from four shape primitives, inspired by cognitive science and Cézanne's compositional view of objects.

The proposed detection pooling (DetPool) mechanism is simple yet effective, and the ablation studies show a large improvement over standard pooling baselines, supporting the importance of object-centric visual representations for generalization.

The empirical evaluation is extensive: simulation scaling studies, real-world Franka experiments on 64 YCB objects, and H1-2 humanoid dexterous-hand experiments. The real-world 67% success rate on YCB is a strong result for a policy trained only on toys.
The paper includes useful scaling analyses, ablations on primitives, toy complexity, model size, condition/prediction length, and robustness tests (lighting, clutter, distractor objects, mask noise).
Reproducibility is strong: code, checkpoints, dataset, demonstration videos, and detailed hardware/teleoperation/printing instructions are provided.
weaknesses: The comparison to OpenVLA-OFT is potentially unfair because the baselines use delta joint control while LEGO uses absolute joint control, and the paper's own ablation shows absolute control is substantially better (80.00 vs 37.02 at 2500 demos). This confounds the main baseline comparison.

The DetPool ablation may conflate the benefit of having an object segmentation mask with the benefit of the specific pooling mechanism. Standard pooling baselines likely do not receive the same object mask, so the large gap may primarily show that object-centric masking helps rather than that DetPool is uniquely effective.

The method depends on an external target-object segmentation/mask at test time. In simulation, ground-truth masks are used; in the real world, a detector trained on 200 toy images feeds SAM 2. It is unclear how target objects are specified and whether the detector generalizes reliably to novel YCB objects, especially in cluttered scenes.

The abstract and introduction overclaim by saying LEGO outperforms state-of-the-art approaches that rely on more in-domain data. Table 2 shows finetuned π0-FAST achieves 76.56% versus LEGO's 66.67%, so the strongest baseline is actually better on the real Franka YCB benchmark.

The H1-2 dexterous-hand evaluation is small-scale: 13 objects, 5 trials each, and hardware issues with the Inspire hands. It lacks confidence intervals and is not as statistically robust as the Franka evaluation.

The novelty of DetPool itself is limited; it is essentially masked attention plus mean pooling over object tokens. The stronger contribution is the toy-training paradigm and empirical demonstration, so the paper's framing around DetPool may overstate the methodological novelty.
